source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 25 2026, ANSWERS.md, HabitAt rounds 1–3): HabitAt was made at the UWUX Design Sprint 2025, a two-hour event in June 2025, and won 1st place. The organizers gave both the HMW (“How might we make a boring everyday task feel rewarding and engaging through gamification?”, used word for word as the heading) and the persona Jasmine (528:4504; the source typos “Paint Points”, “i.e” and “calendars study apps” are fixed in the copy, the wording kept). Team: Amna, Andrew, Anita and Winston; Winston “did most things”, so the copy credits him with most of the design, not all of it, and doesn’t split credit by screen. Deliverables: a clickable prototype and a live demo pitch. In his words, the screens are “a higher quality mid fidelity rather than a complete high fidelity design because of the time constraints”; the copy calls it a polished mid-fidelity prototype, plainly, with no apology. Why a house: chores already belong to rooms, so the house sorts them; a house you can see fill up and grow is the visual progress Jasmine wants; it’s fun and familiar. The number on each room is the tasks left in that room; AI sorts a new task into its room, so New Task asks only for a name and a due date (no room picker). Points: finishing tasks earns points, spent on furniture and on new or bigger rooms that grow the house; the Smaller House (525:3829, no Master Bedroom) is your house before a new room. Friend Map: see friends’ houses and keep each other on track (Jasmine’s peer accountability). The full ideas list (528:4507: 525:2887 features, 525:2888 pages) is shown as two sticky-note boards, including ideas that weren’t designed, with no comment on them. Lessons he chose: rewards you can see; scope to the clock (in two hours, design the core loop first: add a task, finish it, spend the points). Hero: Welcome, Your Home (centre), Living Room; the cover is his current thumbnail, kept as is. Placeholders are cleaned in portfolio-only copies at his request (the Figma file is unchanged and was only read); the replacement chore names (“Vacuum the rug”, “Water the plants”, “Wipe the table”, “Sweep the floor”) are made up and aren’t quoted as event fact; “Clean room” and “Wash dishes” are his own text. Not shown: the reference screenshots 525:2743 and 525:2744 (other people’s illustrations). Not stated, because no source gives them: the exact date, who designed which screen, judge feedback, why household chores were chosen as the task, the horizontal scroll to the smaller house on Home, what each Friend Map pin stands for, and any order of work. Design facts (layouts, prototype wiring, the Smart Animate welcome) come from the Figma page 524:1432 (research10/habitat.md).

fields.title: HabitAt
fields.description: House-shaped chore app, 1st place at UWUX Design Sprint.
fields.intro: HabitAt is an app concept that turns your chores into a house: each room holds its tasks, and finishing them earns points for furniture and new rooms. In a team of four, I did most of the design, and we won 1st place at the UWUX Design Sprint 2025.
fields.summary: Turning a two-hour sprint prompt into a clickable prototype for a chore app where tasks live in the rooms of a house.
fields.overview: HabitAt is for people like Jasmine, the student persona that came with the prompt, who struggles with chores and finds mundane tasks unmotivating unless there’s a sense of reward or fun. Amna, Andrew, Anita and I had two hours, and we submitted a clickable prototype and a live demo pitch.

details.label: Event
details.value:
UWUX Design Sprint 2025
Two hours · June 2025

cover.alt: An iPhone showing the HabitAt home: a house of six coloured rooms with a number on each, a 30 pts cloud, a picket fence and lawn with a New Task button, and the Home, Shop and Friend Map tabs

hero.alt: Three HabitAt screens on iPhones: Welcome to HabitAt over a giant colour-block house, Your Home with its six-room house, and the Living Room with its tasks and furniture

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we make a boring everyday task feel rewarding and engaging through gamification?
content: This was the prompt at the UWUX Design Sprint 2025, and four of us had two hours to answer it. The organizers gave us a persona with it, Jasmine:

bullets: **Background:** a 20-year-old undergraduate university student living in a shared apartment.
**Tech familiarity:** high. She uses her smartphone daily for social media, calendars and study apps.
**Motivators:** visual progress, streaks, mini-rewards, instant gratification and peer accountability.

**Pain points:** she struggles with managing daily chores and routines (cleaning, laundry, organizing), is easily distracted or overwhelmed by schoolwork and social life, and finds mundane tasks unmotivating unless there’s a sense of reward or fun.

sections.title: Idea
sections.heading: A house full of chores
content: We took household chores as our boring everyday task, and listed the features and pages an app for them could have:

notes.text: Sort new tasks automatically with AI
Bad weather and an angry avatar when you don’t do your tasks
Room view: shows a room in your house
Map view: find the houses of your friends
Task view: shows all your tasks and lets you mark them as completed
Add task view: title + due date
Shop view: furniture you can buy
Avatar customization view: choose a human, cat or dog, for now

content.caption: Our list of features and pages.

content: Most of the list hangs on one picture: your home, drawn as a house. We centred the app on a house for three reasons:

bullets: **Chores already belong to rooms,** so the house sorts them for you.
**You can see it fill up and grow.** That’s the visual progress Jasmine wants.

sections.title: Home
sections.heading: Your chores, room by room
content: In HabitAt, your chores are a house. Your Home draws it as six coloured rooms: Laundry and Bathroom under the roof, then the Master Bedroom, Dining Room, Office and Living Room.
The number on each room is how many tasks are left in it. Your points sit in a cloud at the top, New Task sits on the lawn under the picket fence, and the tab bar holds Home, Shop and Friend Map.

content.alt: An iPhone showing Your Home: a house of six coloured rooms (Laundry, Bathroom, Master Bedroom, Dining Room, Office and Living Room), each with a number in a white circle, a 30 pts cloud, a picket fence on a green lawn with a New Task button, and the Home, Shop and Friend Map tabs

sections.title: Tasks
sections.heading: Inside a room
content: Each room holds its own to-do list. Tap the Living Room on the house, and you see the tasks left in it, with the room’s furniture drawn large below them. The green × takes you back home.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: Your Home, then the Living Room opened from it, with a 3 Tasks pill, three chores with empty tick circles, a large couch, TV and cabinet, a green close button and New Task
content.caption: From the house into the Living Room.

content: The Dining Room uses the same layout in its own colour: pink, with a table and two chairs.

content.alt: An iPhone showing the Dining Room in pink: a 3 Tasks pill, three chores in white, a table and two chairs, a green close button and New Task

content: New Task asks for only two things: a name and a due date. There’s no room to pick, because AI sorts each new task into its room. That’s the AI idea from our features list.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: Your Home, then the New Task sheet over the dimmed house, with Enter task name, a Due date field with a calendar icon, a green Save button and the keyboard

sections.title: Rewards
sections.heading: Points you can live in
content: Finishing a task earns points, and points are how the house grows. Your balance sits in the same cloud on Home and in the Shop, which has two tabs.
Furniture sells pieces for your rooms, like a table or a pair of chairs, each priced in points.

content.alt: An iPhone showing the Shop on the Furniture tab: a 30 pts cloud and a grid of tiles for a table at 8 pts and two chairs at 4 pts
content.caption: The Furniture tab, priced in points.

content: On the Rooms tab, you spend points on new or bigger rooms. Choose a room’s size and colour, and tap + to make it bigger, from a 1x2 room to a 2x2.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: the Shop’s Rooms tab with an orange 1x2 Room, a small plus button, six colour swatches with orange ticked and a Done button; then the same tab with a taller 2x2 Room

content: Each new room changes the house itself. On the left is your house before a new room; on the right, a Master Bedroom has joined it, below Laundry and Bathroom.

content.alt: Two houses with an arrow: the smaller house with Laundry, Bathroom, Dining Room, Office and Living Room, then the full house with a purple Master Bedroom added under the roof
content.caption: Your house before and after a new room.

sections.title: Friends
sections.heading: Keeping each other on track
content: Jasmine is motivated by peer accountability, and that’s what the third tab is for. Friend Map lets you see your friends’ houses and keep each other on track.
It’s drawn as a small world: green islands on a light blue circle, dotted with pins, with Add Friend at the bottom.

content.alt: An iPhone showing Friend Map: green islands on a light blue circle against dark blue, orange-red pins on two of the islands, an Add Friend button and the tab bar

sections.title: Welcome
sections.heading: Welcome home
content: HabitAt opens on a house before you have one of your own. “Welcome to HabitAt” sits above a giant house built from blocks in the room colours, with Get Started near the bottom.
Tap Get Started, and the house slides up and off the screen as Make an account comes in: an email, a password and Create Account, which takes you to Your Home.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: Welcome to HabitAt above a giant house of colour blocks with a Get Started button, then Make an account with Email and Password fields, a green Create Account button and the keyboard
content.caption: Welcome, then sign-up.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: Results and lessons
content: HabitAt won 1st place at the UWUX Design Sprint 2025. In two hours, we made a polished mid-fidelity prototype, clickable from the welcome screen through sign-up into the house, and presented it in a live demo pitch.

bullets: **Rewards you can see.** Points that turn into furniture and rooms feel more real than a score.
**Scope to the clock.** In two hours, design the core loop first: add a task, finish it, spend the points.

content: HabitAt started from a prompt and a persona. The prompt: make a boring everyday task feel rewarding and engaging through gamification. The persona: Jasmine, a student who struggles with chores and finds mundane tasks unmotivating without a sense of reward or fun. In two hours, our team of four turned her chores into a house.

Each room holds its tasks and shows how many are left, AI sorts new tasks into their rooms, and finished tasks earn points for furniture and for new or bigger rooms that grow the house. A Friend Map lets friends keep each other on track. I did most of the design, and HabitAt won 1st place.
